title: There\x26#39;s a Scientific Reason Why Some Songs Get Stuck in Your Head
titleZh: 为什么有些歌总在大脑里单曲循环
summary:
如果你看过电影《KPop猎魔女团》，那么当你看到“Golden”这个词时，会有什么反应？对于不熟悉这部作品的人来说，可能毫无感觉。但如果你听过电影中的同名歌曲《Golden》，那段旋律或许会立刻在脑海中响起，不断循环。你甚至可能会不由自主地哼出那句歌词：“we’re goin’ up, up, up”。你有过这样的经历吗？如果有，那么你刚刚体验到的，就是所谓的“非自愿音乐想象”，也就是人们俗称的“耳虫”。研究表明，超过90%的人都有过被耳虫缠住的经历，科学家如今正尝试揭开耳虫的运作机制、产生原因、它能告诉我们关于大脑的哪些信息，以及如果想要摆脱它，我们又该怎么做。

来源：科学警告；作者：Emery Schubert；原文发布时间：2025-10-14 21:21:00

paragraphs.contentEn: If you've watched the movie KPop Demon Hunters and see the word "golden", what happens? For those unfamiliar, nothing will come to mind. But if you've heard the song of the same name, you may start hearing a fragment of the tune repeating in your head, over and over. You might even mouth or sing the words "we're goin' up, up, up". Did that happen to you? If so, you just experienced "involuntary musical imagery", colloquially known as an earworm. More than 90% of the population experience earworms, and researchers are beginning to understand how they work, why they happen, what they tell us about the brain, and even how to get rid of them – if you want to.
paragraphs.contentZh: 如果你看过电影《KPop猎魔女团》，那么当你看到“Golden”这个词时，会有什么反应？对于不熟悉这部作品的人来说，可能毫无感觉。但如果你听过电影中的同名歌曲《Golden》，那段旋律或许会立刻在脑海中响起，不断循环。你甚至可能会不由自主地哼出那句歌词：“we’re goin’ up, up, up”。你有过这样的经历吗？如果有，那么你刚刚体验到的，就是所谓的“非自愿音乐想象”，也就是人们俗称的“耳虫”。研究表明，超过90%的人都有过被耳虫缠住的经历，科学家如今正尝试揭开耳虫的运作机制、产生原因、它能告诉我们关于大脑的哪些信息，以及如果想要摆脱它，我们又该怎么做。

paragraphs.contentEn: The humble earworm has taught music psychologists that repeated fragments of music are recycled from the same mental storage location. In Golden, the music accompanying the words "we're goin' up, up, up" is repeated several times. The most earworm-inducing feature is "contiguous" repetition: a fragment of the music that repeats immediately and without delay, like the repeating chorus of a pop song. Baby Shark, Kylie Minogue's Can't Get You Out Of My Head, and many, many other songs contain such repetition, and have gone through periods of mass exposure – another important ingredient for earworms because it increases familiarity.
paragraphs.contentZh: 耳虫这种看似平常的现象，却让音乐心理学家们意识到：那些在脑海中挥之不去的旋律片段，其实都是从大脑中同一个记忆储存区域反复调用出来的。以歌曲《Golden》为例，伴随歌词“we’re goin’ up, up, up”的旋律在这首歌中多次重复。而最容易引发耳虫的特征之一，就是所谓的“连续重复”：即旋律片段在毫无间隔的情况下立刻再次出现，就像流行歌曲中反复出现的副歌部分那样。《Baby Shark》、凯莉·米洛的《Can’t Get You Out of My Head》，以及无数其他歌曲都采用了这种重复结构，并在某个时期被大量传播——这种高频曝光同样是促成耳虫的重要因素，因为它能提升我们对旋律的熟悉度。

paragraphs.contentEn: When a song becomes an earworm, the mind repeats the musical phrase, seemingly indefinitely. That's because the way music recall is organised in the mind is not like a sound file or tape recording that plays from beginning to end. Rather, the music is efficiently organised into "pockets" based on familiarity and similarity, with some pockets recycled where possible. Exposure to the music binds the various pockets together through the mental network, not unlike a series of instructions: "start with this introduction, play the verse through twice, then go to the chorus and repeat it four times, go to the next section, back to the verse, repeat that", and so on. These "instructions" are a crucial part of the earworm story.
paragraphs.contentZh: 一旦某首歌变成一条耳虫，大脑会似乎无止境地反复播放那段旋律。这是因为，大脑储存音乐的方式，并不像音频文件或磁带那样从头到尾顺序播放。相反，它会根据熟悉度和相似性，将音乐高效地切分成若干“片段”，并在可能的情况下反复调用其中某些片段。随着我们反复聆听同一首曲子，大脑会通过内在的心智网络将这些片段串联起来，形成一套类似“播放指令”的流程：“从这段前奏开始，主歌播放两遍，再进入副歌并重复四次，然后转入下一段，再回到主歌，如此循环”。而正是这些内在的“播放指令”，构成了耳虫现象的关键机制。

paragraphs.contentEn: Several triggers can initiate an earworm: recently having heard some or all of the song, or even just hearing or seeing a relevant phrase (like in this article), or hearing another song that sounds similar. Habits and environmental triggers can play a role too. For example, if you're on the bus listening to music every morning, a song fragment might jump into your head one morning even if your playlist is off.
paragraphs.contentZh: 引发耳虫的原因有很多：可能是你最近刚听过那首歌的全部或部分旋律，也可能只是听到或看到一个相关的词句（就像本文开头提到的例子），又或是听到了另一首旋律相似的歌曲。此外，个人习惯和周围环境也可能成为诱因。比如，如果你习惯每天早晨在公交车上听音乐，那么即便某天没有打开播放列表，某段熟悉的旋律也可能会突然在脑海中响起。

paragraphs.contentEn: There's a deeper reason for this. Earworms are more likely to start their musical wriggles when a particular set of brain regions is activated, called the default mode network. The network is associated with daydreaming and mind-wandering, allowing intrusive and repetitive thoughts to surface more easily. When it comes to song recall, this network is like a naughty, antisocial sibling who picks their favourite part of the song and spends all night in their room listening to it, over and over again.
paragraphs.contentZh: 这一现象背后，其实还有更深层的神经机制。耳虫现象最容易在一组被称为“默认模式网络”（default mode network）的脑区被激活时出现。在白日梦和走神时，这个网络通常也会被激活，会让一些不受控制、反复出现的念头更容易浮现。当大脑回忆起歌曲时，该网络就像一个顽皮、我行我素的少年，专挑自己最喜欢的那段旋律，关起门来不厌其烦地单曲循环。

paragraphs.contentEn: The parts of the brain involved in focused attention that know how many times the song fragment should be played – and what should come next – are locked out of the default mode network's room. When a song has strong repetition, that becomes the network's focus. The instructions for mentally replaying the song become more akin to "when you reach the end of the fragment, go back and play it again", with the "correct" number of repetitions and the other parts of the song nowhere to be seen. The mind is freewheeling, circling around the repeated fragment with no reason to stop.
paragraphs.contentZh: 此时，大脑中负责控制注意力的区域，也就是那些能够判断旋律片段该重复多少次、以及接下来该播放什么的部分，被“默认模式网络”彻底挡在门外。如果一首歌本身具有强烈的重复特征，那么这个片段就会成为该网络的注意中心。此时，大脑的“播放指令”更像是“当这一段结束后，从头再来一遍”，而原本“应有的”重复次数和歌曲的其他部分，则被完全忽略。于是，思绪开始不受控制地围绕着那段旋律不断打转，没有理由停下。

paragraphs.contentEn: Some researchers have found people enjoy their earworms, but there are also reports of song fragments being stuck in people's heads for hours and even days. What if you've just had enough of Golden? To evict an unwanted earworm, you need to disengage your default mode network. One method is to sing the song aloud to other people. The social engagement deters the network from activating, but at the expense of some embarrassment. So … effective, but not always optimal.
paragraphs.contentZh: 一些研究人员发现，人们对耳虫现象并不反感，甚至享受它带来的体验，但也有报告指出，这些旋律片段可能在脑海中盘踞数小时，甚至几天不散。那么，如果你已经彻底听腻了《Golden》，该怎么办？想摆脱这种挥之不去的旋律，关键在于让“默认模式网络”暂时停工。其中一个有效的方法是：对着别人把这首歌大声唱出来。这样的社交互动能抑制该网络的活跃状态，不过代价可能是些许尴尬。所以……这种方法虽然管用，却未必是最佳选择。

paragraphs.contentEn: Another approach is to replace the song by another, less repetitive one, to keep the looping desires of the default mode network at bay. Happy Birthday and God Save the King are examples of songs that don't have the kind of repetition that suits earworms. Software company Atlassian even published a 40-second audio track that's supposed to squash earworms, based on the principles explained above. With such a tune, there is no contiguous repetition for the earworm to hook on to.
paragraphs.contentZh: 另一种办法，是用一首重复性较弱的歌曲来“覆盖”脑海中的旋律，从而抑制“默认模式网络”反复循环的冲动。比如《生日快乐》或《天佑国王》，它们的旋律结构中都缺乏那种容易触发耳虫的连续重复。软件公司Atlassian甚至还发布过一段用来“赶走”耳虫的40秒音轨，据称正是基于上述原理设计。这类曲子中没有任何无缝衔接的重复片段，让耳虫无从附着。

paragraphs.contentEn: Earworms are providing insights into how music is organised, but they can also bring pleasure by repeating the music you're enjoying. If you have a bad relationship with those pesky sound loops, and none of the above tips worked, here's a final bit of advice. Listen to lots of different music and grow to love your inner earworm.
paragraphs.contentZh: 耳虫现象不仅揭示了音乐在大脑中是如何被组织的，有时也能通过循环你喜爱的旋律带来愉悦。不过，如果你实在受不了这些挥之不去的循环旋律，而且前面提到的办法都无济于事，那么还有最后一个建议。多接触不同类型的音乐，尝试欣然接纳、甚至喜欢上你脑海中的那条小耳虫。
